questions.question: Why should AI-Assisted Documentation be taught as a workflow instead of only as tool awareness?
options: Because AI-generated runbooks are always technically accurate once they read fluently
Because teams need shared signals, controls, and decision rules they can apply to real work
Because a polished writing style is sufficient proof that every documented command still works
Because one successful incident response means the documentation needs no more checks
questions.explanation: The lesson is built around reusable operating artifacts — shared signals, controls, decision rules — not the idea that fluent prose proves accuracy, that polish proves a command works, or that one clean incident retires the need for checks.

questions.question: In the lesson's opening example, why did the AI-generated runbook slow the team down during an actual incident?
options: It had no source citations, so the review cadence process rejected it before publication
One command in it was obsolete and a prerequisite step was missing, though the prose read as polished
The owner-approval step was skipped entirely, so the document was never assigned a maintainer
A stale date on the page confused readers about which of several incident runbooks to open first, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
questions.explanation: The lesson's runbook example failed because one command was obsolete and a prerequisite was missing — a command-validation gap, not a citation, approval, or date-labeling problem.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce for AI-Assisted Documentation?
options: A finished runbook that is automatically republished after every code change
A single trust score with no explanation of which check it failed
A word count comparing the AI draft to the previous documentation version
A ranked plan with category, score, priority, controls, and rationale
questions.explanation: The lesson's Python artifact outputs a ranked plan — category, score, priority, controls, and rationale — not an auto-republishing runbook, an unexplained trust score, or a word-count comparison.

questions.question: Which control belongs to the lesson design?
options: Publishing a fluent-sounding draft without assigning an owner to keep it current
Source citation, so every claim in the doc links back to code, tickets, or an architecture decision
Skipping command validation entirely because the runbook's prose already reads as authoritative, before defining the measurement, acceptance threshold, or rollback path
Treating a document's polish as proof that its prerequisites are still accurate
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls include source citation — tying every claim back to code, tickets, or an architecture decision — the opposite of shipping a fluent draft with no owner, skipping command validation, or trusting polish as proof of accuracy.

questions.question: When should a scenario become a launch-gate discussion rather than a casual awareness exercise?
options: When impact, uncertainty, and matched risk signals such as missing ownership are all running high
Only when the documentation happens to be written in a formal and highly technical tone
Only when the runbook covers more than a dozen interdependent production services at once
Never — a documentation gap can always wait until the next scheduled review cadence comes round again
questions.explanation: High-impact, uncertain, risk-heavy documentation gaps need a launch gate regardless of tone, how many services are covered, or whether a review is already scheduled.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the output template?
options: To formally replace the reviewer's sign-off on whether a given runbook is safe to use
To keep the known documentation gaps hidden from the on-call team in the middle of an incident
To create a reusable checklist or prompt that teams can keep applying after the course ends
To automatically generate completion certificates for participants once the workshop ends
questions.explanation: The output template is meant to become a reusable checklist or prompt teams keep applying — not a substitute for reviewer sign-off, a way to hide gaps from on-call, or an automatic certificate generator.
